title: Cost Segregation Study Cost & Fees | AE Tax
primary_keyword: how much does a cost segregation study cost
secondary_keywords: cost segregation pricing; study and Form 3115 fees
meta_description: Compare cost segregation study fees, filing costs, and scope. See AE's published pricing and the questions to ask before signing.
body_markdown:
# How Much Does a Cost Segregation Study Cost?

A cost segregation quote should tell you what you are buying, who will complete the work, and what happens when the report is finished. The study price is only one part of the decision. An inexpensive report can become an expensive engagement if the tax-return work is excluded and no one has agreed to implement it.

AE's published study pricing is **$1 per square foot with a $2,000 minimum per study**. Cost segregation is separately priced from advisory. Your written proposal controls the property scope and any additional work. See the current [cost segregation service page](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study/).

## Compare the complete engagement

Ask each provider to price the same property and deliverables:

| Work | Question to resolve |
|---|---|
| Property study | Which buildings and improvements are included? |
| Prior depreciation review | Will the report reconcile to my existing schedule? |
| Catch-up calculation | Is the calculation included if prior returns are involved? |
| Return implementation | Who updates the depreciation records and prepares any filings? |
| State analysis | Are federal and state differences addressed? |
| Later questions | What support is included if my preparer needs clarification? |

A quoted catch-up calculation does not establish that Form 3115 preparation and filing are included. Put those responsibilities in writing before accepting the proposal.

## Test value using an incremental benefit

Ask for a comparison with the depreciation you would claim without the study. If an illustrative model shows $18,000 of current federal tax reduction and a $4,000 total study-and-implementation cost, the initial difference is $14,000. That simplified subtraction excludes state effects, future tax consequences, and the timing of payment. It is a screening exercise, not a property estimate.

If the deduction cannot be used now, the current benefit may be much smaller. Review [deduction usability and planning](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-resources/) before deciding a quoted deduction justifies the fee.

## What to send for a useful quote

Start with the property type, square footage, purchase date, service date, ownership entity, renovation history, and expected sale date. Identify whether the property has an existing depreciation schedule or came through an exchange. Explain what help you need after the study.

You should leave the comparison with a defined scope, a total proposed cost, and a named party responsible for implementation.

[Talk with AE Tax Advisors about your property and the required scope](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Is Cost Segregation Worth It for a Small Rental? | AE
primary_keyword: is cost segregation worth it for a small rental property
secondary_keywords: cost segregation break-even; rental study return on investment
meta_description: Test whether a cost segregation study makes sense for a smaller rental using usable deductions, total fees, and your expected holding period.
body_markdown:
# Is Cost Segregation Worth It for a Small Rental Property?

For a smaller rental, evaluate cost segregation by the benefit you can use and the full cost of obtaining it. A purchase-price cutoff cannot answer that question on its own. Two owners with similar houses can reach different decisions because their income, records, tax limitations, and sale plans differ.

## Build a three-scenario comparison

Ask your advisor to prepare a baseline without a study, a study scenario using supported property assumptions, and a downside scenario in which some benefit is delayed. Keep acquisition assumptions consistent across all three.

Write down:

- Additional depreciation compared with the baseline.
- Additional deduction usable in the current year.
- Modeled federal and state tax changes.
- Study, implementation, and additional filing costs.
- Expected holding period and modeled sale consequences.

The baseline is essential. A large deduction figure may include depreciation you would receive anyway.

## A hypothetical break-even exercise

Suppose a proposed study creates $20,000 of additional depreciation usable this year. At an assumed 30% marginal rate, a simplified federal benefit is $6,000. If the full engagement costs $3,000, the initial margin is $3,000 before other tax effects.

Now assume only $5,000 of that additional deduction is usable this year. Under the same simplified assumptions, the current benefit becomes $1,500. The remaining deduction may have future value, but it does not fund today's fee.

These are decision examples, not estimates of how much a small rental will reclassify. Start with the [AE calculator](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-calculator/) only after understanding its assumptions.

## When to pause the purchase of a study

Pause if no one has examined your existing depreciation, the projected benefit depends on unsupported asset percentages, or the quote leaves implementation unresolved. A near-term sale also deserves its own comparison. Review [cost segregation before selling](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-before-selling-property/).

For small properties, a useful consultation may conclude that the work should wait. That can be a sound result when your records are incomplete or another property presents a better opportunity.

## Make the decision with your actual numbers

Bring the closing statement, depreciation schedule, approximate current income, and expected holding period. Request a clear explanation of which assumptions are known, which require further study, and which could change the recommendation.

[Ask AE to discuss the economics of your rental](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation and W-2 Income: STR Questions | AE
primary_keyword: can cost segregation offset W2 income
secondary_keywords: STR depreciation W2 income; material participation cost segregation
meta_description: Can cost segregation offset W-2 income? Review STR activity classification, material participation, and loss limits before counting on tax savings.
body_markdown:
# Can Cost Segregation Offset W-2 Income?

Cost segregation alone does not establish that a rental loss can offset W-2 income. The study addresses asset costs and depreciation. Your tax return must separately establish how a loss is treated and whether you can deduct it.

For short stays, the IRS describes exceptions to rental-activity treatment, including an average customer-use period of seven days or less. An applicable exception does not itself establish material participation. The participation analysis and other loss limitations still matter. See [IRS Publication 925](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p925).

## Separate three questions

Ask your advisor to answer these in order:

1. What depreciation does the property support?
2. What activity classification applies to its actual operation?
3. Which losses can this taxpayer use against which income?

A report that answers the first question cannot substitute for the other two. Neither an Airbnb listing nor a management agreement supplies the complete answer.

## Prepare an operating file

Provide reservation records that show customer-use periods, owner and spouse work records, the management contract, and a description of work performed by cleaners, contractors, and managers. Identify personal-use dates separately.

Instead of submitting a reconstructed total such as “about 120 hours,” organize the evidence by task, date, property, and supporting record. Ask the advisor which activities count under the relevant test and which need different treatment.

Read AE's [STR tax strategy guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/str-tax-loophole/) alongside its [Airbnb cost segregation page](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-airbnb/).

## Ask for a usable-loss model

Have the advisor distinguish calculated depreciation, allowed current deductions, and amounts carried forward. Ask what facts could change the result. Include state treatment and any other limitations relevant to the ownership structure.

A hypothetical $100,000 depreciation amount is not a $100,000 reduction in taxes. Even a simplified estimate using a marginal rate is meaningful only after the deductible amount is established.

## Before closing on an STR

Resolve the participation plan before relying on tax benefits in the purchase budget. If a full-service operating arrangement leaves you with little actual work, describe that accurately. Buying a property based on a tax assumption you cannot substantiate can distort the investment decision.

[Discuss your income, rental operations, and participation records with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation With a Property Manager | AE Tax
primary_keyword: cost segregation with a property manager
secondary_keywords: STR material participation property manager; managed Airbnb depreciation
meta_description: Hiring a property manager changes the STR participation analysis. Organize owner work, manager duties, and records before projecting tax benefits.
body_markdown:
# Can You Use Cost Segregation With a Property Manager?

A property manager does not prevent a property from being studied. It does change the facts your advisor needs when evaluating whether a resulting loss is usable. Keep the asset study and the participation review connected throughout the engagement.

Some material-participation tests compare your work with work performed by other people. The IRS lists seven tests, each with its own conditions. A blanket “100 hours is enough” promise can omit a critical comparison. Review [IRS Publication 925](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p925).

## Put responsibilities beside actual work

Create a working table with four columns: task, person responsible, actual time, and supporting record. Include guest communication, pricing, maintenance coordination, bookkeeping, and other work relevant to the operation. Your advisor should decide how each task is treated.

A contract may assign pricing to you while the manager performs it in practice. Record actual work. An unsigned duty list is weaker evidence than messages, completed tasks, and contemporaneous operating records.

## Questions for the manager

Before relying on a participation strategy, ask:

- Can the manager describe the services actually performed?
- How are employee and contractor responsibilities documented?
- Which tasks remain with the owner?
- What records can be supplied for an advisor's review?

Do not assume the manager tracks hours in the form your tax preparer needs. Resolve the records process early.

## A hypothetical owner decision

An owner buys an STR and expects to handle pricing and maintenance coordination. Three months later, the manager takes over both. The original planning assumptions no longer describe the operation.

The useful next step is to update the advisor with the changed facts. It is not to keep using an old projection because the study is already paid for. See AE's [STR guidance](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/str-tax-loophole/).

## Request two separate outputs

Ask for the property depreciation analysis and a written explanation of the participation assumptions used in the tax model. Identify who is responsible for gathering missing facts and when the model will be updated.

The study may remain relevant even if your current deduction is limited. The planning question becomes when and how the depreciation affects your return. Review [AE's planning resources](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-resources/).

[Talk through your manager's scope and your actual role with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation for Older Rentals: Form 3115 | AE
primary_keyword: cost segregation on property purchased years ago
secondary_keywords: lookback cost segregation; catch-up depreciation study
meta_description: Review cost segregation for an older rental, including prior depreciation, catch-up calculations, filing procedure, and implementation responsibilities.
body_markdown:
# Can You Do Cost Segregation on a Property Purchased Years Ago?

An older property's depreciation deserves review when its asset records may not reflect the appropriate classifications. Start with what was acquired, when it entered service, and what has already been reported. The date you order a study does not rewrite the property's history.

Form 3115 requests a change in accounting method or the treatment of an item. Whether a depreciation correction belongs on Form 3115, an amended return, or another procedure depends on the facts and applicable rules. See the [IRS Form 3115 resource](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-3115).

## Build the historical record first

Gather acquisition documents, every available depreciation schedule, improvement records, prior elections, and ownership changes. Identify assets previously sold, replaced, or deducted separately.

Do not send only the latest schedule if it omits earlier disposals or corrections. A year-by-year file helps the preparer understand how today's numbers developed.

Use AE's [document checklist](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-documents-checklist/) to organize the packet.

## Ask how the catch-up amount was calculated

For an applicable method change, the preparer should explain the Section 481(a) calculation and its connection to prior depreciation. Ask for an asset-level reconciliation rather than a single unexplained adjustment.

The review should identify the original dates, applicable depreciation treatment, amounts previously accounted for, and any excluded assets. A new purchase-year assumption should not be applied to an old asset without analysis.

## Clarify the filing assignment

Your proposal should identify who prepares the study, who determines the correction procedure, who calculates the adjustment, and who files the required documents. A report provider may not be your return preparer.

Ask the preparer to check the currently applicable automatic-change procedures and eligibility conditions. A form number alone does not establish that your change qualifies or that the filing is complete. The [Form 3115 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i3115) are a procedural starting point.

## Make the planning decision before paying for the work

Explain whether a sale, refinance, ownership change, or filing deadline is approaching. Request an estimate of the full engagement and the information still needed to evaluate current benefit.

[Ask AE to discuss your property's depreciation history and implementation scope](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation and 100% Bonus Depreciation | AE
secondary_keywords: 100 percent bonus depreciation real estate; old property bonus depreciation
meta_description: Understand how 2026 bonus depreciation affects cost segregation, why acquisition dates matter, and which assumptions your advisor must verify.
body_markdown:
# Cost Segregation and Bonus Depreciation in 2026

Cost segregation and bonus depreciation answer different questions. Cost segregation examines component classifications. Bonus depreciation determines whether eligible assets receive an additional first-year deduction under the applicable rules.

IRS Notice 2026-11 addresses permanent 100% additional first-year depreciation for eligible property acquired after January 19, 2025. Eligibility, service dates, acquisition rules, and elections still require review. The building and land do not become fully deductible merely because a study is performed. See [the IRS announcement and Notice 2026-11](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/treasury-irs-issue-guidance-on-the-additional-first-year-depreciation-deduction-amended-as-part-of-the-one-big-beautiful-bill).

## Give each acquisition its own timeline

Make a table listing the purchase agreement, acquisition date, service date, later improvements, and relevant elections. Keep furniture acquired later separate from the original building purchase.

For a property purchased in 2022, a study ordered in 2026 does not make its components newly acquired in 2026. Ask the advisor to explain which historical rules apply and whether any correction procedure is needed.

## Ask what is included in the estimate

A projection should identify the assets assumed eligible for bonus depreciation and the costs left in other categories. Request explanations for items that depend on additional documentation.

An estimate using a standard reclassification percentage can help explore sensitivity, but it cannot establish what your property supports. See the disclosed assumptions in [AE's calculator](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-calculator/).

## Review existing elections

Provide copies of depreciation and business-interest elections. The IRS explains that an electing real property trade or business must use ADS for residential rental property, nonresidential real property, and qualified improvement property, with consequences for bonus eligibility. Do not assume the same treatment for every asset in the study. See [IRS business-interest election guidance](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/questions-and-answers-about-the-limitation-on-the-deduction-for-business-interest-expense).

## Separate eligibility from usefulness

After identifying eligible assets, ask how much resulting deduction is usable on your return and how the federal model compares with state treatment. Have the preparer compare the result with ordinary depreciation and future sale assumptions.

Review [AE's study services](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study/) for scope, then [discuss your acquisition dates and elections with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation Before Selling a Rental | AE Tax
secondary_keywords: cost segregation short holding period; depreciation recapture planning
meta_description: Compare cost segregation before a property sale using usable deductions, sale tax, total fees, and the time between deduction and closing.
body_markdown:
# Should You Do Cost Segregation Before Selling a Property?

If you expect to sell soon, evaluate cost segregation with a purchase-to-sale tax model. The first-year deduction is only one part of that model. Study fees, implementation costs, timing, and sale consequences can materially change the result.

Depreciation affects adjusted basis, and dispositions may produce recapture or other special tax treatment. Different assets can have different consequences. See [IRS Publication 544](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p544).

## Compare two complete paths

Ask your advisor for a no-study path and a study path using the same sale assumptions. Both should include expected closing date, sale price, transaction costs, relevant allocations, tax rates, and existing carryforwards.

Show the anticipated cash effects by year. A benefit received years before sale has different economics from a deduction obtained shortly before closing.

## Use an illustrative holding-period test

Suppose a model shows $25,000 of earlier tax reduction, $5,000 of study and implementation costs, and $18,000 of additional modeled sale tax. The undiscounted difference is $2,000 before other effects. That is a narrow margin if the assumptions are uncertain.

If the sale moves forward or the current deduction is limited, the answer may change. This example does not predict any property's recapture amount; it shows why comparing only the fee with the upfront deduction is incomplete.

## Keep the proposed sale allocation visible

Give the advisor the expected treatment of furnishings, equipment, improvements, and the building. Ask which items require valuation support and how the asset register will connect with closing records.

Do not wait until closing to discover that the study and sale documents describe the property differently. Coordinate the preparer, study provider, and transaction team while there is time to resolve questions.

## What to bring to AE

Bring the existing depreciation schedule, expected sale date, draft transaction terms if available, and any proposed exchange plan. For older properties, explain the filed-return history. Read [AE's Form 3115 guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/form-3115-cost-segregation/) and [study pricing](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study-cost-pricing/) before defining the engagement.

[Ask AE to compare the current benefit with your planned exit](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation Documents: Close the Gaps | AE Tax
primary_keyword: documents needed for cost segregation study
secondary_keywords: missing cost segregation records; rental improvement invoices
meta_description: Organize acquisition, depreciation, and improvement records for a cost segregation study, with a practical process for resolving missing documents.
body_markdown:
# Documents Needed for a Cost Segregation Study

The most useful cost segregation packet connects your purchase records, property details, prior tax treatment, and later improvements. It also shows what is missing. An organized file saves time because the study provider and preparer can identify unresolved questions before work reaches the filing stage.

## Use four folders and one questions list

Organize your records as follows:

| Folder | Examples |
|---|---|
| Acquisition | Purchase agreement, closing statement, appraisal, allocation support |
| Property | Floor plans, inspection reports, photos, rental-use information |
| Improvements | Contracts, itemized invoices, change orders, completion dates |
| Tax history | Depreciation schedules, relevant returns, prior study and elections |

Then create a questions list with the missing item, why it matters, the person obtaining it, and the next follow-up date.

The packet is a preparation framework. Your provider may request additional information for an exchange, inherited property, partnership, or unusual transaction.

## Reconstruct missing records transparently

An old renovation may have a bank payment but no itemized invoice. Try the contractor, permit office, property manager, inspection file, or archived correspondence. Label reconstructed information so it is not confused with contemporaneous evidence.

Do not convert a remembered estimate into an exact historical cost. Tell the provider what you know, where it came from, and what you cannot confirm. Ask whether further evidence is needed before the proposed classification can be supported.

## Prevent duplicate assets

Identify furniture and equipment already deducted or recorded separately. If a furnished purchase included a separately allocated furniture package, flag that allocation before the building costs are analyzed.

Similarly, distinguish the original property from later improvements. An invoice covering three rentals should retain its property-level allocation.

## Make the handoff reviewable

Keep one shared index of the documents provided and the versions used. When a revised depreciation schedule arrives, note whether it replaces the earlier version and why. This helps the return preparer reconcile the work.

For the next step, review [AE's basis reconciliation guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/blog/cost-segregation-report-basis-reconciliation/) and [study services](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study/).

[Ask AE what records are needed for your property and filing history](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation Report: Questions for Your CPA | AE
primary_keyword: what to do after cost segregation study
secondary_keywords: cost segregation CPA handoff; study tax return implementation
meta_description: Turn a completed cost segregation report into an organized CPA handoff with asset reconciliation, filing assignments, and open questions.
body_markdown:
# What to Do After a Cost Segregation Study Is Finished

When your cost segregation report arrives, the next step is to connect it with your return preparer's work. Sending the PDF without a defined implementation assignment can leave the report unused or create a last-minute filing problem.

## Schedule a report-to-return handoff

Ask the provider and preparer to review the property identity, taxpayer, basis, service dates, and asset schedule together. Keep the report, source records, questions, and implementation decisions in the same property file.

Use a handoff checklist:

- Does the report analyze the correct owner and property?
- Do its totals reconcile to the records the preparer uses?
- Are assets already deducted or separately depreciated identified?
- Are later improvements and removed assets handled explicitly?
- Which assumptions remain unresolved?
- Who will complete each filing and update each schedule?

This is a practical acceptance process, not an assertion that a report has IRS approval.

## Separate report corrections from tax decisions

If the report uses an incorrect service date, ask the provider to correct it. If the question concerns a filing election or the usability of a loss, assign it to the tax preparer or advisor. Record both kinds of decisions so neither disappears into an email thread.

The [IRS cost segregation guide](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p5653.pdf) is an examination resource. It is not a binding pronouncement or certification of a provider.

## Resolve fees and timing

Confirm whether implementation is included in your original proposal. An engineering report, catch-up calculation, return preparation, and continuing advisory can be separate assignments.

If the preparer needs additional time, discuss the available filing options before a deadline passes. Request a specific list of outstanding work instead of assuming receipt of the report means the return is ready.

## Retain a future-use file

Keep the final asset register for later renovations, replacements, and sale planning. Record which version was implemented and retain the explanations behind material changes.

Read [AE's report deliverables guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/blog/cost-segregation-study-audit-ready-deliverables/) and [Form 3115 resource](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/form-3115-cost-segregation/) when preparing the handoff.

[Discuss study implementation and responsibilities with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation Land Allocation: Owner Guide | AE
secondary_keywords: land value depreciation study; purchase price allocation rental
meta_description: Review land allocation before cost segregation. Organize valuation support and reconcile the property purchase before using a depreciation estimate.
body_markdown:
# How Land Allocation Affects a Cost Segregation Study

Land allocation belongs near the beginning of a cost segregation review. Land is not depreciable, and a combined purchase must be allocated appropriately between the assets acquired. The IRS discusses purchase allocations and basis in [Publication 551](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p551).

## Start with the evidence behind the allocation

Gather the closing statement, purchase agreement, appraisal, assessment records, and any allocation previously used on your return. Ask the preparer how those records support the proposed land amount.

The useful question is not which percentage produces the largest deduction. It is which allocation is supportable for this transaction and what additional evidence would resolve uncertainty.

## Show the sensitivity without selecting an answer

Consider an illustrative $600,000 acquisition basis before land. An assumed 15% land allocation leaves $510,000 before further analysis. An assumed 30% allocation leaves $420,000. The $90,000 difference illustrates why the starting allocation matters.

Neither percentage is a recommendation or typical allocation. Do not use this exercise to choose the lower land amount. Use it to recognize which assumption needs evidence before relying on a projection.

## Reconcile unusual purchase packages

A furnished rental, multiple parcels, or a purchase involving business assets may need more than a two-line land-and-building split. Identify the assets described in the contract and any separately stated amounts.

Ask whether the same acquisition dollars appear in a furniture schedule and the building study. A reconciliation should explain where each amount went. The [AE report reconciliation guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/blog/cost-segregation-report-basis-reconciliation/) provides a useful next step.

## Review existing-return differences

If an earlier return used a different allocation, flag that before finalizing the study. Ask the tax preparer to explain the reason for any proposed change and the correct filing treatment. A new report should not silently replace prior numbers.

Keep the underlying evidence with the final report so the allocation remains understandable when the property is refinanced, renovated, or sold.

Use the [document checklist](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-documents-checklist/) to prepare the file, then [talk through unresolved basis questions with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation for Condos: HOA Questions | AE Tax
secondary_keywords: condo HOA cost segregation; townhome depreciation study
meta_description: Prepare a condo cost segregation review with unit records, HOA documents, renovation details, and clear ownership questions for shared amenities.
body_markdown:
# Cost Segregation for Condos and Townhomes: What to Gather

A condo or townhome requires a property-specific review. The unit's name and purchase price do not establish which assets belong in a study. Your records should explain what you acquired, what you later improved, and how shared facilities relate to your ownership.

## Describe the unit separately from the development

Create two lists: items inside or attached to your unit, and facilities shared across the development. Provide the governing documents and ask the provider which ownership interests require further analysis.

A listing that advertises a pool, gym, and landscaped grounds is useful context, but it is not a complete tax allocation. Ask how the report distinguishes the unit, shared property interests, and separately purchased items.

## Identify your renovations

Provide invoices for work you funded, including the location, scope, completion date, and any separately acquired equipment or furniture. Explain which work the association performed and how you were charged.

An assessment labeled “capital project” may leave several questions unanswered. Obtain available project descriptions, statements, and allocation records so your preparer can evaluate the facts.

## Keep rental and personal-use records together

Tell the advisor whether the unit is a long-term rental, short-stay accommodation, or a property you also use personally. Provide a dated use calendar rather than an annual percentage estimated from memory.

The IRS describes special rules for dwelling units used personally and rented in [Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527). A study does not resolve those use questions by itself.

## Compare the scope before comparing the price

Ask whether the quote covers the unit only, later improvements, furnishings, and any supported common-property interests. Confirm what the provider needs from the association and who obtains it.

If another quote appears cheaper, compare exclusions. A proposal based on incomplete ownership records may require additional work later.

Review [AE's study pricing](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study-cost-pricing/) and [documents checklist](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-documents-checklist/). Bring an organized property packet and a list of unresolved HOA questions to the initial conversation.

[Discuss your condo or townhome study scope with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation After Renovation: Owner Guide | AE
secondary_keywords: rental renovation depreciation; repairs versus cost segregation
meta_description: Organize renovation costs before a cost segregation study. Separate project records, prior assets, repairs, and implementation questions.
body_markdown:
# Should You Review Cost Segregation After a Renovation?

A renovation is a useful time to revisit your property records. Before analyzing depreciation categories, determine how the expenditures should be treated. The IRS tangible-property rules distinguish currently deductible expenses from costs that must be capitalized. See [IRS tangible-property guidance](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/tangible-property-final-regulations).

## Break the project into identifiable work

An invoice that says “complete remodel: $85,000” does not explain what happened. Ask for available detail covering demolition, replacement, finishes, equipment, labor, and completion dates.

Preserve before-and-after photographs, contracts, change orders, and descriptions of the old components. Those records make the review more specific than a single project total.

## Ask two separate treatment questions

First ask which expenditures are capitalized and which may receive other treatment. Then ask how capitalized costs should be classified and depreciated. Cost segregation is not a reason to place every project expense into the same category.

Identify work performed before the original rental launch separately from later work. Include service dates for completed phases rather than assuming the full project became usable on the date of the last payment.

## Review removed assets

A replacement can raise questions about the asset that was removed. The IRS examination resource on partial dispositions describes reviewing the disposed portion and its basis. A new improvement does not automatically prove a qualifying disposition. See [the IRS partial-disposition practice unit](https://www.irs.gov/pub/fatca/int_practice_units/examining-tp-electing-partial-disposition.pdf).

Ask the preparer whether a separate disposition analysis is appropriate and what procedural timing applies. Keep that assignment explicit; do not assume it is included in the study quote.

## Close the project file

Reconcile total payments to invoices and explain differences such as deposits, reimbursements, and unfinished work. Note furniture or equipment already recorded separately so it is not included twice.

Use [AE's document checklist](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-documents-checklist/) to assemble the file and [study services](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study/) to discuss the scope.

[Ask AE to coordinate a renovation and depreciation review](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Compare Cost Segregation Quotes: 10 Questions | AE
primary_keyword: how to compare cost segregation quotes
secondary_keywords: cost segregation provider questions; study scope comparison
meta_description: Compare cost segregation proposals using ten practical questions about evidence, deliverables, implementation, fees, and follow-up support.
body_markdown:
# How to Compare Cost Segregation Quotes

Compare cost segregation quotes by putting the same assignment in front of each provider. A provider promising a larger deduction may be using different assumptions, a different property scope, or a different definition of savings. Resolve those differences before choosing.

## Send a common request

Provide the address, property type, acquisition facts, service date, improvement history, and available depreciation records. State whether you need only a study or also tax implementation.

Ask each firm to distinguish known facts from estimates. Keep its response with the proposed fee so you can understand what the estimate actually includes.

## Ask these ten questions

1. Which taxpayer, parcels, buildings, and improvements does the quote cover?
2. Who performs the property analysis and reviews the final work?
3. What information must I supply before the fee is firm?
4. How will missing records and estimated costs be documented?
5. What final report and asset schedule will I receive?
6. How will the totals reconcile with my existing records?
7. Who determines and completes any filing procedure?
8. Which implementation services are excluded?
9. What follow-up support is included for my tax preparer?
10. What additional fees could arise under this scope?

Write down the answer to each question. A blank answer is an item to resolve directly, not evidence that a provider cannot perform the work.

## Normalize the claimed benefit

Ask whether the estimate describes reclassified basis, depreciation, incremental deductions, or tax savings. Those amounts are different.

For a tax-savings estimate, request the assumed usable deduction, tax rate, state treatment, and comparison baseline. Include expected sale timing if it could affect the economics.

## Compare total proposed costs

Add study fees, required preparer work, proposed corrections, and separately priced state work. If you already have a CPA, confirm the CPA will accept the handoff and quote the implementation.

AE's advisory and property-study services have distinct scopes; the signed proposal should identify the responsible parties.

title: Cost Segregation for Multiple Properties | AE Tax
primary_keyword: cost segregation for multiple rental properties
secondary_keywords: rental portfolio depreciation review; which rental to study first
meta_description: Prioritize cost segregation across a rental portfolio using records, usable deductions, fees, ownership, and expected sale dates.
body_markdown:
# Which Rental Property Should You Study First?

For a rental portfolio, begin with a property-by-property inventory. Ordering a study for every building immediately can spend money before the advisor has identified where the strongest usable benefit may lie.

## Create a portfolio decision sheet

Use one row per property with these fields:

- Owner and tax-return reporting entity.
- Acquisition and service dates.
- Purchase basis and land-allocation support.
- Property use and later improvements.
- Existing depreciation schedule and missing records.
- Expected holding period.
- Estimated study and implementation cost.
- Open questions affecting current deduction usability.

Treat the sheet as an intake tool. It does not establish tax treatment or authorize moving losses between entities.

## Identify blockers before ranking opportunities

One property may have excellent records but a planned sale next quarter. Another may have a longer holding period but incomplete renovation invoices. A third may already have a study that was never implemented.

Those are different assignments. The best first engagement could be implementing an existing report rather than commissioning a new one.

Use [AE's document checklist](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-documents-checklist/) to identify the missing work and [sale planning guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-before-selling-property/) for near-term exits.

## Request coordinated modeling

Ask the advisor to explain how the property-level assumptions connect with the return-level model. Identify the affected taxpayers, relevant limitations, and state filings. Keep any grouping or election questions explicit rather than assuming the portfolio is one tax activity.

If priorities depend on projected income, request an update when that income changes. A ranking based on an earlier forecast can become stale before reports are completed.

## Stage the work deliberately

Agree on the first property, required records, decision owner, and scope. Use the completed handoff to improve the process for the next property. Portfolio efficiency should come from consistent records and coordination, not an assumption that every building has the same asset mix.

See [AE's study services](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study/) for the initial discussion.

[Ask AE to help prioritize your portfolio's depreciation review](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

title: Cost Segregation and State Taxes: Questions | AE
secondary_keywords: state bonus depreciation adjustment; federal state depreciation schedules
meta_description: Ask how cost segregation affects each state return. Keep federal and state depreciation schedules separate when modeling usable tax benefits.
body_markdown:
# Why a Cost Segregation Tax Estimate Needs a State Review

A federal tax estimate is not a complete estimate of your cost segregation benefit. Ask your preparer to verify the rules for each affected state and filing year, including treatment of bonus depreciation, required adjustments, and later recovery of those adjustments.

This guide provides a planning checklist. It does not assert a particular state's conformity position or replace research into current state law.

## List every affected return

Identify where the property is located, where you reside, and which entity owns it. Ask which returns are affected and how the model addresses resident and nonresident reporting.

Do not simply add a state tax rate to a federal rate and apply the result to the report's largest number. The tax base, deduction timing, and interactions may differ.

## Request separate schedules

Ask for a federal depreciation schedule and the applicable state schedules. If the preparer expects an adjustment, request a description of the current-year effect and the records needed to track later years.

Keep those schedules with the final property report. A sale, move, or preparer change can become harder to reconcile if the state history is missing.

## Test the estimate with a hypothetical

Suppose a simplified federal model shows $12,000 of current tax reduction. If a state does not allow the same current deduction under the relevant facts, multiplying that federal deduction by the state rate overstates the immediate combined benefit.

The correct response is to calculate the state result separately. Any delayed benefit should appear in the year it is expected, with the assumptions disclosed. This example illustrates a modeling issue, not the rules of a named state.

## Define who performs the state work

Ask whether the study provider supplies state schedules or whether your preparer creates them. Confirm whether additional state implementation is included in the fee and who retains the adjustment history.

Review [AE's pricing and scope](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-study-cost-pricing/) and [report reconciliation guidance](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/blog/cost-segregation-report-basis-reconciliation/) when preparing those questions.

[Discuss your property state, resident state, and filing responsibilities with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).

body_markdown:
# How Long Does a Cost Segregation Study Take?

A useful cost segregation timeline includes the work required to implement the result. Report delivery is one milestone. Your tax preparer may still need to resolve classifications, reconcile records, determine filing procedures, and update federal and state schedules.

Ask for a property-specific schedule once the provider understands the scope and available records. Do not assume a general turnaround promise applies to an older property with missing schedules or a complex renovation.

## Plan backward from the filing decision

Give the provider and preparer your intended filing date. Ask what must be complete before the return can be prepared, which dates are provisional, and which party controls each step.

Use these milestones:

| Milestone | Completion evidence |
|---|---|
| Scope agreed | Written responsibilities and fee |
| Records accepted | Missing-items list resolved or explicitly addressed |
| Property analysis complete | Draft results ready for review |
| Reconciliation complete | Differences with existing schedules explained |
| Filing procedure determined | Preparer's implementation assignment documented |
| Return work complete | Required schedules and filings prepared |

The table is a planning tool, not a guaranteed delivery schedule.

## Resolve dependencies early

An owner may have closing documents ready while the prior CPA still holds the depreciation history. Another may need a contractor's itemized renovation invoice. Identify those dependencies at engagement rather than when the report is nearly finished.

AE's [document checklist](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/cost-segregation-documents-checklist/) can help prepare the initial packet.

## Keep the year of the deduction separate

Ask your preparer which tax year and filing procedure apply. The date a report arrives does not, by itself, establish the year in which its depreciation belongs. Older-property work may require a different process from a newly placed-in-service property.

Review [AE's Form 3115 guide](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/form-3115-cost-segregation/) if prior depreciation is part of the assignment.

## Agree on a delay plan

Before a deadline approaches, ask what happens if critical records or review work remain outstanding. The preparer should evaluate the filing options under the actual facts. Do not create an artificial rush that leaves assumptions unexplained.

[Discuss your property, records, and intended filing timeline with AE](https://www.aetaxadvisors.com/contact/).
